claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The reassignment of AGG to methionine in a clade of uncultivated Bacilli likely evolved by a change in the amino acid charging of an arginine tRNA.
claims.source: In a clade of uncultivated Bacilli, the reassignment of AGG to become the dominant methionine codon likely evolved by a change in the amino acid charging of an arginine tRNA.
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis of tRNA genes and their identity elements presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The reassignments of CGA and/or CGG were found in genomes with low GC content.
claims.source: The reassignments of CGA and/or CGG were found in genomes with low GC content, an evolutionary force that likely helped drive these codons to low frequency and enable their reassignment.
claims.evidence: Supported by genomic GC content data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Low GC content is an evolutionary force that likely helped drive CGA and CGG codons to low frequency and enable their reassignment.
claims.source: The reassignments of CGA and/or CGG were found in genomes with low GC content, an evolutionary force that likely helped drive these codons to low frequency and enable their reassignment.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed correlation between low GC content and codon reassignment.

claims.claim: The first alternative genetic codes were discovered by comparing newly sequenced genomes to amino acid sequences obtained by direct protein sequencing.
claims.source: The first alternative genetic codes were discovered by comparing newly sequenced genomes to amino acid sequences obtained by direct protein sequencing.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to historical discoveries in the Introduction.

claims.claim: Nonstandard codon translations were found in human mitochondria.
claims.source: Nonstandard codon translations were found this way in human mitochondria (Barrell et al., 1979), Candida yeasts (Kawaguchi et al., 1989), green algae (Schneider et al., 1989), and Euplotes ciliates (Meyer et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Barrell et al., 1979.

claims.claim: Nonstandard codon translations were found in Candida yeasts.
claims.source: Nonstandard codon translations were found this way in human mitochondria (Barrell et al., 1979), Candida yeasts (Kawaguchi et al., 1989), green algae (Schneider et al., 1989), and Euplotes ciliates (Meyer et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Kawaguchi et al., 1989.

claims.claim: Nonstandard codon translations were found in green algae.
claims.source: Nonstandard codon translations were found this way in human mitochondria (Barrell et al., 1979), Candida yeasts (Kawaguchi et al., 1989), green algae (Schneider et al., 1989), and Euplotes ciliates (Meyer et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Schneider et al., 1989.

claims.claim: Nonstandard codon translations were found in Euplotes ciliates.
claims.source: Nonstandard codon translations were found this way in human mitochondria (Barrell et al., 1979), Candida yeasts (Kawaguchi et al., 1989), green algae (Schneider et al., 1989), and Euplotes ciliates (Meyer et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Meyer et al., 1991.

claims.claim: Some reassignments of stop codons to amino acids were detected from DNA sequence alone, based on the appearance of in-frame stop codons in critical genes.
claims.source: Some reassignments of stop codons to amino acids were detected from DNA sequence alone, based on the appearance of in-frame stop codons in critical genes (Yamao et al., 1985; Caron and Meyer, 1985; Cupples and Pearlman, 1986; Keeling and Doolittle, 1996; McCutcheon et al., 2009; Campbell et al., 2013; Záhonová et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Reassignment of the stop codons UAA and UAG to glutamine is the most common change in eukaryotic nuclear genomes, appearing at least five independent times.
claims.source: Reassignment of the stop codons UAA and UAG to glutamine is the most common change in eukaryotic nuclear genomes, appearing at least five independent times (Schneider et al., 1989; Keeling and Doolittle, 1996; Keeling and Leander, 2003; Karpov et al., 2013; Swart et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: In bacteria, all of the known changes reassign the stop codon UGA to either glycine in the Absconditabacteria and Gracilibacteria or tryptophan in the Mycoplasmatales, Entomoplasmatales and several insect endosymbiotic bacteria.
claims.source: In bacteria, all of the known changes reassign the stop codon UGA to either glycine in the Absconditabacteria and Gracilibacteria (Campbell et al., 2013; Rinke et al., 2013) or tryptophan in the Mycoplasmatales, Entomoplasmatales (Bové, 1993), and several insect endosymbiotic bacteria (McCutcheon et al., 2009; McCutcheon and Moran, 2010; Bennett and Moran, 2013; Salem et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Codetta uses profile hidden Markov models (HMMs) from the Pfam database to infer codon decodings.
claims.source: With Codetta, we extend this idea to systematic high-throughput analysis by using a probabilistic modeling approach to infer codon decodings and by taking advantage of the large collection of probabilistic profiles of conserved protein domains (profile HMMs) in the Pfam database (El-Gebali et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology of Codetta.

claims.claim: The Pfam database contains over 17,000 profile HMMs of conserved protein domains from all three domains of life.
claims.source: The Pfam database contains over 17,000 profile HMMs of conserved protein domains from all three domains of life, which are expected to align to about 50% of coding regions in a genome (El-Gebali et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to El-Gebali et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Pfam profile HMMs are expected to align to about 50% of coding regions in a genome.
claims.source: The Pfam database contains over 17,000 profile HMMs of conserved protein domains from all three domains of life, which are expected to align to about 50% of coding regions in a genome (El-Gebali et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to El-Gebali et al., 2019.

claims.claim: About 8–34 aligned consensus columns suffice for >95% power to infer the correct amino acid for a codon in E. coli.
claims.source: Depending on the codon, we found that about 8–34 aligned consensus columns suffice for >95% power to infer the correct amino acid.
claims.evidence: Supported by subsampling analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Codetta predicted CUG translation consistent with the known phylogenetic distribution of CUG reassignments in 453 out of 462 yeast species.
claims.source: For 453 species, the predicted CUG translation was consistent with the known phylogenetic distribution of CUG reassignments (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: Supported by analysis of yeast genomes and Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Candida albicans CUG codons are stochastically decoded as a mix of serine (97%) and leucine (3%).
claims.source: In some CUG-Ser clade species, such as Candida albicans, CUG codons are stochastically decoded as a mix of serine (97%) and leucine (3%) because the CUG-decoding tRNACAG is aminoacylated by both the seryl- and leucyl-tRNA synthetases (Suzuki et al., 1997; Gomes et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Suzuki et al., 1997 and Gomes et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Codetta predicted C. albicans to use the predominant serine translation for CUG.
claims.source: This includes C. albicans, which was predicted to use the predominant serine translation (Gomes et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Supported by Codetta analysis and citation to Gomes et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Saccharomycopsis malanga expresses both serine and leucine tRNACAG genes.
claims.source: We used northern blotting to assay the expression of both tRNACAG genes in some of these species under a variety of growth conditions (data not shown), but could detect reliable expression of both serine- and leucine-type tRNACAG genes only in Saccharomycopsis malanga (only the serine tRNACAG could be detected in other species) (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: Supported by northern blotting data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Both serine and leucine S. malanga tRNACAG are predominantly charged in cells.
claims.source: We found that both serine and leucine S. malanga tRNACAG are predominantly charged in cells (Figure 2C), likely partaking in the translation of CUG codons.
claims.evidence: Supported by acid urea PAGE northern blotting data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Codetta analyzed 251,571 assembled bacterial and archaeal genomes from GenBank.
claims.source: To explore the diversity of genetic codes in bacterial and archaeal genomes, we used Codetta to analyze 251,571 assembled genomes from GenBank, including partial assemblies and those derived from single-cell genomics and metagenomic assembly.
claims.evidence: This describes the dataset analyzed in the study.

claims.claim: 99.79% of sense codon predictions were consistent with the expected amino acid in the dereplicated bacterial and archaeal dataset.
claims.source: Across the 48,693 genomes (dereplicated to one assembly per species), we predicted the amino acid translation of a total of 2,970,497 individual sense codons (roughly 61 times the number of genomes), with 99.79% of the predictions consistent with the expected amino acid (similar proportion across bacteria and archaea) (Table 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by data presented in Table 2.

claims.claim: About 0.19% of sense codons had a '?' inference in the dereplicated dataset.
claims.source: About 0.19% of sense codons had a '?' inference, demonstrating that entire genomes contain more than enough information to infer the amino acid translation of most sense codons.
claims.evidence: Supported by data presented in Table 2.

claims.claim: 612 sense codons were predicted to have unexpected amino acid meanings in the dereplicated dataset.
claims.source: Unexpected amino acid meanings were predicted for 612 sense codons.
claims.evidence: Supported by data presented in Table 2.

claims.claim: 99.80% of stop codons had no inferred amino acid meaning in the dereplicated dataset.
claims.source: For stop codons, 99.80% out of a total of 145,855 stop codons across the dereplicated bacterial and archaeal genomes had no inferred amino acid meaning, as expected.
claims.evidence: Supported by data presented in Table 2.

claims.claim: The most common error was the inference of AGA and/or AGG arginine codons as coding for lysine, occurring in 567 bacterial species.
claims.source: The most common error was the inference of AGA and/or AGG arginine codons as coding for lysine, occurring in 567 bacterial species.
claims.evidence: This describes a systematic error identified in the analysis.

claims.claim: The unusually high GC content of genomes with AGA/AGG lysine inference (ranging between 0.52 and 0.77, median 0.68) suggests the source of the lysine inference may come from high GC content-driven nonsynonymous substitutions.
claims.source: The unusually high GC content of these genomes (ranging between 0.52 and 0.77, median 0.68) suggests that the source of the lysine inference may come from high GC content-driven nonsynonymous substitutions of the AAA and AAG lysine codons to AGA and AGG arginine codons at protein residues that can tolerate either positively charged amino acid.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on observed GC content patterns.

claims.claim: Eight bacterial genomes were inferred to translate AGG, a canonical arginine codon, as methionine.
claims.source: Eight bacterial genomes were inferred to translate AGG, a canonical arginine codon, as methionine.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claims.claim: All eight AGG-to-methionine genomes were assembled from fecal metagenomes of baboons or humans.
claims.source: All eight genomes were assembled from fecal metagenomes of baboons or humans (Parks et al., 2017; Almeida et al., 2019) and have only coarse-grained NCBI genome classification as uncultured Bacillales or Mollicutes bacteria.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Parks et al., 2017 and Almeida et al., 2019.

claims.claim: In the AGG-to-methionine reassigned clade, AGG is the dominant methionine codon with a usage of 209–235 per 10,000 codons in Pfam alignments.
claims.source: In the reassigned clade, AGG is the dominant methionine codon with a usage of 209–235 per 10,000 codons in Pfam alignments, outnumbering the canonical methionine codon AUG (59–69 per 10,000 codons) (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: Supported by codon usage data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The tRNACCU from the AGG-to-methionine reassigned clade has features of methionine identity and lacks the important arginine identity element A20 in the D-loop.
claims.source: The cognate tRNA for the AGG codon, tRNACCU, from the reassigned clade has features of methionine identity (including an A73 discriminator base and G2:C71 and C3:G70 base pairs in the acceptor stem) and lacks the important arginine identity element A20 in the D-loop (Meinnel et al., 1993; Giegé et al., 1998), supporting translation of AGG as methionine (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: Supported by tRNA sequence analysis shown in Figure 3C and citations to Meinnel et al., 1993 and Giegé et al., 1998.

claims.claim: The reassigned methionine tRNACCU likely emerged through a change in aminoacylation of an arginine tRNACCU rather than through duplication and anticodon mutation of a methionine tRNA.
claims.source: This implies that the reassigned and outgroup tRNACCU evolved from the same ancestral tRNA gene, and the reassigned methionine tRNACCU likely emerged through a change in aminoacylation of an arginine tRNACCU rather than through duplication and anticodon mutation of a methionine tRNA.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on genomic context and tRNA gene analysis.

claims.claim: Two phage assemblies were predicted to translate AGG as methionine.
claims.source: We inferred the genetic code of phage genomes assembled by Al-Shayeb et al., 2020 from the same baboon fecal metagenomic dataset as some reassigned Bacilli genomes. Two phage assemblies were predicted to translate AGG as methionine (assemblies GCA_902730795.1 and GCA_902730815.1).
claims.evidence: Supported by Codetta analysis of phage genomes.

claims.claim: The four CGA/CGG candidate reassignments share very low genomic GC content (0.26–0.38).
claims.source: The four CGA/CGG candidate reassignments share several features that suggest common evolutionary forces at play. Most notable is the very low genomic GC content of the reassigned clades (0.26–0.38, Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Supported by genomic GC content data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: In all four CGA/CGG reassignment clades, the usage of GC-rich CGN-box codons is depressed and arginine residues are primarily encoded by AGA codons.
claims.source: In all four clades, the usage of GC-rich CGN-box codons – including CGA and CGG – is depressed and arginine residues are primarily encoded by AGA codons (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: Supported by codon usage data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: In the three Firmicute CGG reassignments, CGG is an extremely rare codon (codon usage <6 per 10,000 in aligned Pfam domains for all species).
claims.source: In the three Firmicute CGG reassignments, CGG is an extremely rare codon (codon usage <6 per 10,000 in aligned Pfam domains for all species).
claims.evidence: Supported by codon usage data.

claims.claim: A shared feature of the three Firmicute CGG reassignments is that the tRNAUCG is missing.
claims.source: A shared feature of the three Firmicute CGG reassignments is that the tRNAUCG is missing (Figure 4B), presumably lost prior to or during the reassignment of CGG.
claims.evidence: Supported by tRNA gene analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Low genomic GC content is thought to be created by mutational bias in favor of AT nucleotides, causing a gradual shift towards synonymous codons with lower GC compositions.
claims.source: Low genomic GC content is thought to be created by mutational bias in favor of AT nucleotides, causing a gradual shift towards synonymous codons with lower GC compositions (Knight et al., 2001b; Muto and Osawa, 1987).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Knight et al., 2001b and Muto and Osawa, 1987.

claims.claim: Most UGA reassignments in bacteria occur in clades with very low genomic GC content.
claims.source: Most UGA reassignments in bacteria occur in clades with very low genomic GC content, which is thought to have reduced UGA to very low usage in favor of the stop codon UAA.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on observed patterns in the data.

claims.claim: The Mycoplasmatales and Entomoplamatales have genomic GC content of 0.24–0.39.
claims.source: This includes the Mycoplasmatales and Entomoplamatales (0.24–0.39 GC) (Jukes, 1985; Bové, 1993), Absconditabacteria and Gracilibacteria (0.21–0.53 GC, Figure 4—source data 1; Campbell et al., 2013; Rinke et al., 2013), and most insect endosymbiotic bacterial reassignments (0.13–0.17 GC, except for Hodgkinia cicadicola with 0.28–0.58 GC) (McCutcheon and Moran, 2010; Bennett and Moran, 2013; Salem et al., 2017; Campbell et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Jukes, 1985 and Bové, 1993.

claims.claim: Absconditabacteria and Gracilibacteria have genomic GC content of 0.21–0.53.
claims.source: This includes the Mycoplasmatales and Entomoplamatales (0.24–0.39 GC) (Jukes, 1985; Bové, 1993), Absconditabacteria and Gracilibacteria (0.21–0.53 GC, Figure 4—source data 1; Campbell et al., 2013; Rinke et al., 2013), and most insect endosymbiotic bacterial reassignments (0.13–0.17 GC, except for Hodgkinia cicadicola with 0.28–0.58 GC) (McCutcheon and Moran, 2010; Bennett and Moran, 2013; Salem et al., 2017; Campbell et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 4—source data 1 and citations to Campbell et al., 2013 and Rinke et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Most insect endosymbiotic bacterial reassignments have genomic GC content of 0.13–0.17, except for Hodgkinia cicadicola with 0.28–0.58.
claims.source: This includes the Mycoplasmatales and Entomoplamatales (0.24–0.39 GC) (Jukes, 1985; Bové, 1993), Absconditabacteria and Gracilibacteria (0.21–0.53 GC, Figure 4—source data 1; Campbell et al., 2013; Rinke et al., 2013), and most insect endosymbiotic bacterial reassignments (0.13–0.17 GC, except for Hodgkinia cicadicola with 0.28–0.58 GC) (McCutcheon and Moran, 2010; Bennett and Moran, 2013; Salem et al., 2017; Campbell et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to McCutcheon and Moran, 2010; Bennett and Moran, 2013; Salem et al., 2017; Campbell et al., 2015.

claims.claim: All five of the new reassignments affect arginine codons (AGG, CGA, and CGG).
claims.source: All five of the new reassignments affect arginine codons (AGG, CGA, and CGG).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings.

claims.claim: Several arginine reassignments are known in mitochondria, including AGA and AGG reassigned to serine, glycine, and possibly stop, AGG reassigned to lysine, AGG reassigned to alanine and methionine, and CGG reassigned to leucine.
claims.source: While these are the first instances of arginine codon reassignment in non-organellar genomes, several arginine reassignments are known in mitochondria: in various metazoan mitochondria, the codons AGA and AGG have been reassigned to serine, glycine, and possibly stop and AGG has been reassigned to lysine (Knight et al., 2001a; Abascal et al., 2006a), and in various green algal mitochondria AGG has been reassigned to alanine and methionine and CGG to leucine (Noutahi et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Knight et al., 2001a; Abascal et al., 2006a; Noutahi et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Across the tree of life, arginine has an over-representation of codons in the genetic code relative to usage in proteins.
claims.source: First, across the tree of life, arginine has an over-representation of codons in the genetic code relative to usage in proteins (Jukes et al., 1975; King and Jukes, 1969), contributing to rare usage of the least favored arginine codon.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Jukes et al., 1975 and King and Jukes, 1969.

claims.claim: The six arginine codons range from 1 to 3 GC nucleotides in composition, only equaled by leucine.
claims.source: Second, the six arginine codons range from 1 to 3 GC nucleotides in composition (only equaled by leucine), which may create greater bias in codon usage in response to genomic GC content than for amino acids with less GC variability in their codons.
claims.evidence: This is based on knowledge of the genetic code structure.

claims.claim: In most bacteria, the only widespread instance of inosine tRNA wobble is used to decode the CGU, CGC, and CGA arginine codons.
claims.source: The arginine codon CGG may be even more of a target for reassignment because, in most bacteria, the only widespread instance of inosine tRNA wobble is used to decode the CGU, CGC, and CGA arginine codons (Grosjean et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Grosjean et al., 2010.

claims.claim: In the absence of a tRNAUCG, CGG is decoded by a dedicated tRNACCG and can be reassigned without affecting the translation of other codons.
claims.source: In the absence of a tRNAUCG, CGG is decoded by a dedicated tRNACCG and can be reassigned without affecting the translation of other codons.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on tRNA decoding rules.

claims.claim: CGG to tryptophan reassignment occurred in three bacterial clades.
claims.source: Some codon reassignments have convergently reappeared across the tree of life: CGG to tryptophan in three bacterial clades described here, AGG to methionine in a clade of Bacilli described here and in green algal mitochondria (Noutahi et al., 2019), UGA to tryptophan in multiple bacterial, mitochondrial, and eukaryotic lineages (Knight et al., 2001a), and others.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from the study.

claims.claim: AGG to methionine reassignment occurred in a clade of Bacilli and in green algal mitochondria.
claims.source: Some codon reassignments have convergently reappeared across the tree of life: CGG to tryptophan in three bacterial clades described here, AGG to methionine in a clade of Bacilli described here and in green algal mitochondria (Noutahi et al., 2019), UGA to tryptophan in multiple bacterial, mitochondrial, and eukaryotic lineages (Knight et al., 2001a), and others.
claims.evidence: Supported by findings from the study and citation to Noutahi et al., 2019.

claims.claim: UGA to tryptophan reassignment occurred in multiple bacterial, mitochondrial, and eukaryotic lineages.
claims.source: Some codon reassignments have convergently reappeared across the tree of life: CGG to tryptophan in three bacterial clades described here, AGG to methionine in a clade of Bacilli described here and in green algal mitochondria (Noutahi et al., 2019), UGA to tryptophan in multiple bacterial, mitochondrial, and eukaryotic lineages (Knight et al., 2001a), and others.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Knight et al., 2001a.

claims.claim: The tRNA anticodon-codon pairing rules dictate that U- and C-ending codons cannot be assigned separate meanings.
claims.source: For example, the tRNA anticodon-codon pairing rules dictate that U- and C-ending codons cannot be assigned separate meanings, and indeed this has not been observed in any known genetic codes.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge of tRNA wobble pairing rules.

claims.claim: U- and C-ending codons have not been observed to have separate meanings in any known genetic codes.
claims.source: For example, the tRNA anticodon-codon pairing rules dictate that U- and C-ending codons cannot be assigned separate meanings, and indeed this has not been observed in any known genetic codes.
claims.evidence: This is based on a survey of known genetic codes.

claims.claim: Codetta aligns Pfam profile HMMs to a six-frame standard genetic code translation of the input DNA/RNA sequence using the HMMER hmmscan program.
claims.source: We align Pfam profile HMMs to a six-frame standard genetic code translation of the input DNA/RNA sequence using the HMMER hmmscan program (Eddy, 2011; Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology of Codetta, shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Codetta assigns an amino acid translation to a codon if it attains a decoding probability above 0.9999.
claims.source: We assign an amino acid translation to a codon if it attains a decoding probability above some threshold (typically 0.9999).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology of Codetta.

claims.claim: Codetta assigns a '?' if no amino acid decoding satisfies the probability threshold.
claims.source: We assign a '?' if no amino acid decoding satisfies the probability threshold (including the case where '?' itself has high probability).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology of Codetta.

claims.claim: For 453 yeast species, the predicted CUG translation was consistent with the known phylogenetic distribution of CUG reassignments.
claims.source: For 453 species, the predicted CUG translation was consistent with the known phylogenetic distribution of CUG reassignments (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: Supported by Codetta analysis and Figure 2A.

claims.claim: For nine yeast species, Codetta did not put a high probability on any amino acid decoding of CUG.
claims.source: For the remaining nine species, Codetta did not put a high probability on any amino acid decoding of CUG (inferred meaning of '?').
claims.evidence: Supported by Codetta analysis.

claims.claim: Babjeviella inositovora and Cephaloascus fragrans are basal members of the CUG-Ser clade.
claims.source: Two of these species – Babjeviella inositovora and Cephaloascus fragrans – are basal members of the CUG-Ser clade.
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: Both B. inositovora and C. fragrans genomes contain a CUG-decoding tRNACAG gene with features of serine identity.
claims.source: Both of these genomes contain a CUG-decoding tRNACAG gene with features of serine identity (see Materials and methods) and B. inositovora has previously been shown to translate CUG codons primarily as serine by whole proteome mass spectrometry (Krassowski et al., 2018; Mühlhausen et al., 2018), suggesting that CUG is decoded as serine in these species.
claims.evidence: Supported by tRNA gene analysis.

claims.claim: B. inositovora has been shown to translate CUG codons primarily as serine by whole proteome mass spectrometry.
claims.source: Both of these genomes contain a CUG-decoding tRNACAG gene with features of serine identity (see Materials and methods) and B. inositovora has previously been shown to translate CUG codons primarily as serine by whole proteome mass spectrometry (Krassowski et al., 2018; Mühlhausen et al., 2018), suggesting that CUG is decoded as serine in these species.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Krassowski et al., 2018 and Mühlhausen et al., 2018.

claims.claim: 10 out of 11 species in the Ascoidea and Saccharomycopsis clade encode two types of tRNACAG genes, one predicted to be serine-type and one leucine-type.
claims.source: Analysis of tRNA genes revealed that 10 out of 11 species in this clade encode two types of tRNACAG genes, one predicted to be serine-type and one leucine-type, suggesting that CUG may be ambiguously translated as both serine and leucine via competing tRNAs in some of these species (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: Supported by tRNA gene analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Ambiguous translation of CUG was demonstrated in Ascoidea asiatica.
claims.source: The existence of serine and leucine tRNACAG genes in some Ascoidea and Saccharomycopsis yeasts was reported by Krassowski et al., 2018 and Mühlhausen et al., 2018 while we were conducting experiments. Ambiguous translation of CUG was demonstrated in Ascoidea asiatica (Mühlhausen et al., 2018); however, for S. malanga only expression of the serine tRNACAG could be detected (Krassowski et al., 2018) and incorporation of predominantly serine at protein positions encoded by CUG (Mühlhausen et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Mühlhausen et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The GTDB assigns the eight AGG-to-methionine genomes to a three species clade within the placeholder genus UBA7642.
claims.source: The GTDB assigns these eight genomes to a three species clade within the placeholder genus UBA7642 (family CAG-288, order RFN20, class Bacilli), of which all other species were inferred to translate AGG as arginine (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: Supported by GTDB phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: In each of the AGG-to-methionine reassigned genomes, the AGG inference by Codetta is based on over 2200 aligned Pfam consensus columns from over 480 different Pfam domains.
claims.source: In each of the reassigned genomes, the AGG inference by Codetta is based on a sufficiently large number of aligned Pfam consensus columns (over 2200 compared to an average of about 1800 for each of the other 60 sense codons) from over 480 different Pfam domains.
claims.evidence: This describes the evidence supporting the AGG reassignment inference.

claims.claim: The three residues that contact the anticodon nucleotides in A. aeolicus MetRS, which are conserved through all domains of life, remain unchanged in the reassigned clade MetRS sequence.
claims.source: The three residues that contact the anticodon nucleotides in A. aeolicus, which are conserved through all domains of life (Nakanishi et al., 2005), also remain unchanged in the reassigned clade MetRS sequence (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citation to Nakanishi et al., 2005.

claims.claim: The reassigned Bacilli genomes use an arginine-type tRNAUCU to decode the unaffected AGA arginine codon.
claims.source: The reassigned genomes use an arginine-type tRNAUCU to decode the unaffected AGA arginine codon.
claims.evidence: Supported by tRNA gene analysis.

claims.claim: In E. coli, the U34 of tRNAUCU is modified to 5-methylaminomethyluridine.
claims.source: In E. coli, the U34 of tRNAUCU is modified to 5-methylaminomethyluridine (Sakamoto et al., 1993), which primarily decodes the AGA codon with a low level of AGG recognition (Spanjaard et al., 1990).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Sakamoto et al., 1993 and Spanjaard et al., 1990.

claims.claim: Mukai et al., 2015 demonstrated that it is possible to engineer separate decodings for AGA and AGG in E. coli by reducing expression level of the tRNAUCU.
claims.source: Mukai et al., 2015 demonstrated that it is possible to engineer separate decodings for AGA and AGG in E. coli by reducing expression level of the tRNAUCU to the point where decoding of AGG by tRNAUCU is presumably insignificant in competition with the cognate tRNACCU.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Mukai et al., 2015.

claims.claim: In the reassigned Bacilli clade, the preferred arginine codon is CGU.
claims.source: In most outgroup genomes, AGA is the dominant arginine codon, while in the reassigned clade the preferred arginine codon is CGU (Figure 3A), which may indicate reduced demand and expression of tRNAUCU to avoid ambiguous translation of AGG.
claims.evidence: Supported by codon usage data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The genus Peptacetobacter is predicted to translate CGG as glutamine.
claims.source: Three clades are in the phylum Firmicutes: the genus Peptacetobacter is predicted to translate CGG as glutamine (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), a clade of uncultivated Bacilli in the GTDB order RFN20 (same as the AGG-reassigned Bacilli) is predicted to translate CGG as tryptophan (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and members of the genus Anaerococcus are also predicted to translate CGG as tryptophan (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by Codetta analysis and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: A clade of uncultivated Bacilli in the GTDB order RFN20 is predicted to translate CGG as tryptophan.
claims.source: Three clades are in the phylum Firmicutes: the genus Peptacetobacter is predicted to translate CGG as glutamine (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), a clade of uncultivated Bacilli in the GTDB order RFN20 (same as the AGG-reassigned Bacilli) is predicted to translate CGG as tryptophan (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and members of the genus Anaerococcus are also predicted to translate CGG as tryptophan (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by Codetta analysis and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Members of the genus Anaerococcus are predicted to translate CGG as tryptophan.
claims.source: Three clades are in the phylum Firmicutes: the genus Peptacetobacter is predicted to translate CGG as glutamine (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), a clade of uncultivated Bacilli in the GTDB order RFN20 (same as the AGG-reassigned Bacilli) is predicted to translate CGG as tryptophan (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and members of the genus Anaerococcus are also predicted to translate CGG as tryptophan (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by Codetta analysis and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Absconditabacteria is predicted to have reassigned CGA and CGG both to tryptophan.
claims.source: The fourth clade is Absconditabacteria (also known as Candidate Division SR1, part of the Candidate Phyla Radiation), which is predicted to have reassigned CGA and CGG both to tryptophan (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), in addition to the already known reassignment of UGA from stop to glycine.
claims.evidence: Supported by Codetta analysis and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Absconditabacteria has a known reassignment of UGA from stop to glycine.
claims.source: The fourth clade is Absconditabacteria (also known as Candidate Division SR1, part of the Candidate Phyla Radiation), which is predicted to have reassigned CGA and CGG both to tryptophan (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), in addition to the already known reassignment of UGA from stop to glycine.
claims.evidence: This is a previously known finding.

claims.claim: In one Absconditabacteria, the frequency of both CGA and CGG approaches the frequency of the canonical tryptophan codon UGG.
claims.source: In one Absconditabacteria (assembly GCA_002791215.1), the frequency of both CGA and CGG approaches the frequency of the canonical tryptophan codon UGG, consistent with a more advanced stage of codon reassignment (usage of CGA and CGG is 30 and 24 per 10,000, compared to 35 for UGG).
claims.evidence: Supported by codon usage data.

claims.claim: Some Gracilibacteria were predicted to translate CGG as tryptophan, while others translate CGG as arginine.
claims.source: The CGG reassignment in the Absconditabacteria may extend to members of the sister clade Gracilibacteria – some Gracilibacteria were predicted to translate CGG as tryptophan, while others translate CGG as arginine (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: Supported by Codetta analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: The closest sister group to Peptacetobacter has extremely rare usage of CGG (<1 per 10,000 in aligned Pfam domains in all but two species) and appears to lack any tRNA capable of decoding CGG by standard codon-anticodon pairing rules.
claims.source: For the CGG reassignment in Peptacetobacter, the closest sister group (which includes the pathogen Clostridioides difficile) has extremely rare usage of CGG (<1 per 10,000 in aligned Pfam domains in all but two species) and appears to lack any tRNA capable of decoding CGG by standard codon-anticodon pairing rules (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by codon usage and tRNA gene analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In Anaerococcus, all species contain a CGG-decoding tRNACCG with features of tryptophan identity.
claims.source: In Anaerococcus, all species contain a CGG-decoding tRNACCG with features of tryptophan identity (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Supported by tRNA gene analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Members of the outgroup genus Finegoldia also have a tRNACCG with features of tryptophan identity.
claims.source: Unexpectedly, members of an outgroup genus Finegoldia also have a tRNACCG with features of tryptophan identity (CGG inferred to be '?' by Codetta).
claims.evidence: Supported by tRNA gene analysis.

claims.claim: Codetta validated on the budding yeasts (Saccharomycetes, 462 sequenced species) that vary in their translation of CUG as either serine, leucine, or alanine.
claims.source: We further validated Codetta on the budding yeasts (Saccharomycetes, 462 sequenced species) that vary in their translation of CUG as either serine, leucine, or alanine depending on the species (Mühlhausen et al., 2016; Krassowski et al., 2018; Mühlhausen et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Mühlhausen et al., 2016; Krassowski et al., 2018; Mühlhausen et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Codetta cannot predict reassignment to a noncanonical amino acid.
claims.source: Since Codetta selects the most likely amino acid translation among the 20 canonical amino acids, some types of codon reassignments may be missed. We cannot predict reassignment to a noncanonical amino acid – for such codons, Codetta would pick the nonspecific model or an amino acid that is used similarly in other species.
claims.evidence: This is a limitation of the method.

claims.claim: Codetta cannot directly detect ambiguous translation.
claims.source: We also cannot directly detect ambiguous translation, which may represent an important stage in codon reassignment.
claims.evidence: This is a limitation of the method.

claims.claim: Codetta cannot detect the use of new start and stop codons or context-dependent stop codons.
claims.source: Since we do not model translational initiation and termination, we cannot detect the use of new start and stop codons or context-dependent stop codons that also possess an amino acid meaning, known to occur in some eukaryotes (Swart et al., 2016; Heaphy et al., 2016; Záhonová et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a limitation of the method, with citations to examples in eukaryotes.

claims.claim: In the 'codon capture' model, the codon is first driven to near extinction by pressures unrelated to reassignment, such as biased genomic GC content or genome reduction.
claims.source: In the 'codon capture' model, the codon is first driven to near extinction by pressures unrelated to reassignment, such as biased genomic GC content or genome reduction, which then minimizes the impact of reassignment on protein translation (Osawa and Jukes, 1989).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Osawa and Jukes, 1989.

claims.claim: The codon capture model was first proposed for the reassignment of the stop codon UGA to tryptophan in Mycoplasma capricolum.
claims.source: This model was first proposed for the reassignment of the stop codon UGA to tryptophan in Mycoplasma capricolum, whose low genomic GC content (25% GC) in combination with small genome size (1 Mb) was thought to have driven the stop codon UGA to extremely low usage in favor of UAA and allowed 'capture' of UGA by a tryptophan tRNA (Bové, 1993; Osawa and Jukes, 1989).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Bové, 1993 and Osawa and Jukes, 1989.

claims.claim: In the 'ambiguous intermediate' model, a codon is decoded stochastically as two different meanings in an intermediate step of codon reassignment.
claims.source: In the 'ambiguous intermediate' model, a codon is decoded stochastically as two different meanings in an intermediate step of codon reassignment, and this translational pressure induces codon substitutions at positions where ambiguity is deleterious (Schultz and Yarus, 1994; Massey et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Schultz and Yarus, 1994 and Massey et al., 2003.

claims.claim: Yeasts translate the codon CUG as both leucine and serine by stochastic tRNA charging or by competing tRNA species.
claims.source: Extant examples of ambiguous translation support the plausibility of this model, such as yeasts that translate the codon CUG as both leucine and serine by stochastic tRNA charging (Gomes et al., 2007) or by competing tRNA species (Mühlhausen et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Gomes et al., 2007 and Mühlhausen et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The 'tRNA loss-driven reassignment' model proposes an intermediate stage where a codon cannot be translated efficiently, perhaps due to tRNA gene loss or mutation.
claims.source: Alternatively, the 'tRNA loss-driven reassignment' model proposes an intermediate stage where a codon cannot be translated efficiently, perhaps due to tRNA gene loss or mutation, creating pressure for synonymous substitutions specifically away from that codon, allowing it to be captured later by a different tRNA (Mühlhausen et al., 2016; Sengupta and Higgs, 2005).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Mühlhausen et al., 2016 and Sengupta and Higgs, 2005.

claims.claim: Reduction in codon usage driven by genome-wide processes plays a major role in enabling codon reassignment in bacteria.
claims.source: We posit that, in bacteria, reduction in codon usage driven by genome-wide processes plays a major role in enabling codon reassignment and may explain why codon reassignments repeatedly evolve in clades such as Firmicutes (known for their low genomic GC content) and lifestyles such as endosymbiosis (which is often accompanied by genome reduction and low GC content) (McCutcheon and Moran, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on observed patterns in the data, with citation to McCutcheon and Moran, 2011.

results.result: Codetta is a computational method that uses profile HMMs from the Pfam database to infer genetic codes by aligning them to six-frame translations of input sequences and computing decoding probabilities for each codon.
results.evaluation: Claims C16, C17, C18, C60, C62, and C63 collectively describe the Codetta methodology with appropriate citations and methodological details. The approach is clearly documented with specific parameters (e.g., probability threshold of 0.9999) and is supported by the Pfam database characteristics.

results.result: Codetta requires approximately 8-34 aligned consensus columns for >95% power to correctly infer codon meanings in E. coli.
results.evaluation: Claim C19 is supported by subsampling analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, which systematically evaluated the relationship between the number of consensus columns and inference accuracy. The range varies by codon, which is appropriately noted.

results.result: Codetta successfully validated on 462 yeast species, correctly predicting CUG translation consistent with known phylogenetic distributions in 453 species, including the predominant serine translation in C. albicans.
results.evaluation: Claims C21, C23, C64, and C92 are supported by analysis of yeast genomes with appropriate citations to prior work. The validation demonstrates Codetta's ability to recapitulate known genetic code variations, providing confidence in the method's accuracy.

results.result: Saccharomycopsis malanga expresses both serine and leucine tRNACAG genes that are predominantly charged, suggesting ambiguous CUG translation.
results.evaluation: Claims C24, C25, and C69 are supported by northern blotting and acid urea PAGE data shown in Figure 2C. The experimental evidence directly demonstrates expression and charging of both tRNA types, supporting the inference of ambiguous translation.

results.result: Codetta failed to infer CUG translation in nine yeast species, including B. inositovora and C. fragrans, despite evidence these species translate CUG as serine.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C68 acknowledge a limitation of Codetta in detecting CUG translation in certain species. The failure is explained by inconsistent amino acid conservation at aligned positions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and is supported by independent mass spectrometry evidence for serine translation in B. inositovora.

results.result: Codetta analyzed 251,571 bacterial and archaeal genomes, achieving 99.79% accuracy for sense codons and 99.80% accuracy for stop codons in a dereplicated dataset of 48,693 species.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C26-C30 describe the large-scale genomic survey with specific accuracy metrics supported by Table 2. The high accuracy rates and low '?' inference rates demonstrate the method's robustness across diverse genomes.

results.result: The most common Codetta error was inferring AGA/AGG arginine codons as lysine in 567 bacterial species with high GC content (0.52-0.77), likely due to GC-driven nonsynonymous substitutions.
results.evaluation: Claims C31 and C32 identify a systematic error and provide a mechanistic explanation based on GC content analysis. The correlation between high GC content and this specific error pattern is well-reasoned, though the explanation remains inferential.

results.result: Eight bacterial genomes from uncultivated Bacilli were discovered to translate AGG as methionine, with AGG becoming the dominant methionine codon (209-235 per 10,000 codons).
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C33-C35, C71, and C72 describe a novel genetic code discovery supported by extensive computational evidence (>2200 aligned Pfam columns from >480 domains) and phylogenetic analysis using GTDB. The high usage of AGG as methionine indicates an established reassignment.

results.result: The AGG to methionine reassignment in Bacilli likely evolved through changes in aminoacylation of an arginine tRNACCU, which acquired methionine identity elements while losing arginine identity element A20.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C36, C37, C74, and C75 provide a mechanistic explanation supported by tRNA sequence analysis (Figure 3C), genomic context analysis (Figure 3D), and MetRS sequence conservation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). The evidence converges on aminoacylation change rather than anticodon mutation.

results.result: Two phage assemblies from the same metagenomic dataset were predicted to translate AGG as methionine, suggesting phage adaptation to the host's alternative genetic code.
results.evaluation: Claim C38 is supported by Codetta analysis of phage genomes. The finding is consistent with phage adaptation to host translation machinery, though experimental validation would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Four clades with CGA/CGG reassignments share very low genomic GC content (0.26-0.38), depressed CGN-box codon usage, and in three Firmicute clades, loss of tRNAUCG.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C39-C42 describe common features across multiple reassignments supported by GC content data (Figure 4A), codon usage analysis (Figure 4B), and tRNA gene analysis. The convergent patterns suggest shared evolutionary mechanisms.

results.result: Four new CGA/CGG reassignments were discovered: CGG to glutamine in Peptacetobacter, CGG to tryptophan in two Bacilli clades and Anaerococcus, and CGA/CGG to tryptophan in Absconditabacteria.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C82 describe novel genetic code discoveries supported by Codetta analysis and supplementary figures showing phylogenetic context, tRNA genes, and multiple sequence alignments. However, the rarity of these codons means predictions are based on fewer aligned columns, increasing uncertainty.

results.result: Low GC content driven by mutational bias is proposed as a major evolutionary force enabling codon reassignment in bacteria by reducing codon usage to low frequency.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C43, C44, and C101 present an evolutionary model supported by observed correlations between low GC content and codon reassignments, with appropriate citations to prior work. The inference is well-reasoned but remains correlative rather than causative.

results.result: All five new bacterial reassignments affect arginine codons, which are predisposed to reassignment due to codon over-representation, GC variability (1-3 GC nucleotides), and unique tRNA decoding patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C53 synthesize findings and provide mechanistic explanations for why arginine codons are reassignment targets. The arguments are supported by citations to prior work on codon usage and tRNA wobble rules, though some aspects remain speculative.

results.result: Some codon reassignments have convergently evolved multiple times: CGG to tryptophan in three bacterial clades, AGG to methionine in Bacilli and green algal mitochondria, and UGA to tryptophan in multiple lineages.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C56 document convergent evolution of genetic code changes, supported by findings from this study and appropriate citations to prior work. The patterns suggest either shared evolutionary processes or constraints from conserved translational machinery.

results.result: Analysis of outgroup species reveals potential intermediate stages of codon reassignment, including rare CGG usage without decoding tRNAs and variable CGG translation in Gracilibacteria.
results.evaluation: Claims C84, C88-C91 describe observations in outgroup species that may represent evolutionary intermediates. The evidence includes codon usage data and tRNA gene analysis, though the evolutionary interpretations remain inferential.

results.result: Codetta has limitations: it cannot predict reassignment to noncanonical amino acids, cannot directly detect ambiguous translation, and cannot detect new start/stop codons or context-dependent stop codons.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C95 honestly acknowledge methodological limitations. These are logical consequences of the method's design (selecting among 20 canonical amino acids, assuming unambiguous translation, not modeling initiation/termination).

results.result: Historical context: The genetic code was proposed as a 'frozen accident' but alternative genetic codes have been discovered in over 30 lineages through various methods including direct protein sequencing and DNA sequence analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C8-C15 provide historical background supported by appropriate citations to foundational work. These claims establish context for the current study and are well-documented in the literature.

results.result: Three evolutionary models explain codon reassignment: 'codon capture' (codon driven to extinction by GC bias/genome reduction), 'ambiguous intermediate' (stochastic dual decoding), and 'tRNA loss-driven reassignment' (inefficient translation drives substitutions).
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C100 describe established theoretical models with appropriate citations to original work and supporting examples. These models provide framework for interpreting the new discoveries.

results.result: Known UGA reassignments in bacteria occur in clades with low GC content: Mycoplasmatales/Entomoplasmatales (0.24-0.39), Absconditabacteria/Gracilibacteria (0.21-0.53), and insect endosymbionts (0.13-0.17).
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C47 compile GC content data for known reassignments with appropriate citations. This provides comparative context for the new discoveries and supports the GC content hypothesis.

results.result: tRNA anticodon-codon pairing rules dictate that U- and C-ending codons cannot be assigned separate meanings, and this constraint has been observed in all known genetic codes.
results.evaluation: Claims C57 and C58 state an established principle of tRNA wobble pairing supported by knowledge of genetic code structure. This constraint helps explain observed patterns of codon reassignment.

results.result: Ambiguous CUG translation was previously demonstrated in Ascoidea asiatica, while S. malanga was reported to express only serine tRNACAG under different growth conditions.
results.evaluation: Claim C70 cites prior work demonstrating ambiguous translation in A. asiatica and contrasts it with previous findings for S. malanga. The authors note their different growth conditions may explain detection of leucine tRNACAG expression.

results.result: C. albicans CUG codons are stochastically decoded as 97% serine and 3% leucine due to dual aminoacylation of tRNACAG.
results.evaluation: Claim C22 describes a well-established example of ambiguous translation supported by citations to Suzuki et al., 1997 and Gomes et al., 2007. This provides context for understanding ambiguous translation mechanisms.

results.result: In E. coli, tRNAUCU is modified to 5-methylaminomethyluridine and primarily decodes AGA with low AGG recognition; the reassigned Bacilli clade shows reduced AGA usage and preference for CGU, potentially avoiding ambiguous AGG translation.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 combine established knowledge about E. coli tRNA modification with observations about codon usage in the reassigned clade. The inference about avoiding ambiguous translation is reasonable but speculative.
